title: Each charge and its form
statement: A sentence must be imposed for each offence; the maximum and any scheme (category, standard sentence, mandatory minimum) follow the offence; representative and rolled-up charges have special rules; summary jurisdiction and the two-year summary cap turn on the class of offence; an inchoate offence is not a standard sentence offence and a relative maximum needs the primary offence; the CCE scheme turns on Schedule 1A and transaction values; federal charges are outside scope. Several gates turn on per-charge classes that the register does not carry and the Manual lists only for some offence chapters (e.g. 27.5.1, 28.7; a schedule 1 sexual offence for a DATO; a Schedule 1 offence for forfeiture); otherwise, without a stated class the gate must caution, not decide silently from the offence name (for a DATO on a 24.1.1, 24.1.2 or 24.1.4 offence the app also does not propose one unless the user states it is not a schedule 1 sexual offence: flag.dato_sexual_offence_scope). Historic provisions not in the register (e.g. ss 45(2A), 47A) carry Category 1 status, for an offender 18 or older, for offending from 20 March to 30 June 2017 (cat1.historic_sexual_provisions).

title: Status at the time of offending and sentences being served
statement: Offending on parole or bail, prison offences and escape engage presumptions of cumulation; offending on conditional liberty or contrary to orders may aggravate; totality applies to sentences being served. An offender serving the non-parole period of a prior sentence needs a new single non-parole period (with the allowance for the parole sentence served and no double-counted pre-sentence detention); no term may be cumulated on a life sentence imposed, being served or paroled from; an offender serving a Commonwealth sentence needs a commencement direction within the s 16(4) limit. Orders in force at sentencing limit what can be imposed: the CCO maximum term and total hours, youth detention maxima across occasions, one DATO at a time and no DATO for an offender on parole or subject to a higher-court sentence, a previous AEO for the offence, concurrency of licence orders; CCO conditions must fit any intervention orders.

statement: The statutory gravity factors and the offence-specific guidance require these facts; mandatory minimum schemes turn on gross violence or single punch features proved beyond reasonable doubt and on the offender’s role; some maxima are higher only if a statutory condition is established.

refs.q: The Act prescribes a number of non-exclusive circumstances relevant to determining the gravity of offending, including: • its nature and gravity; • the offender’s culpability and degree of responsibility for the offence; • whether the offending was motivated, wholly or partly, by hatred or prejudice against a group of people with whom the victim was associated or the offender believed they were associated; • its impact on the victim; • the circumstances of the victim; • any injury, loss, or damage resulting directly from the offending; • any aggravating or mitigating circumstances of the offender; • ‘or of any other relevant circumstances’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors

refs.q: The use of a weapon is relevant to assessing the gravity of the offending. While there are few limits on what might be considered a ‘weapon’, the more dangerous the item and the greater its capacity to invoke fear, the greater the seriousness of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances > 5.2.8.1 – Weapons

refs.q: Manslaughter in circumstances of gross violence requires proof beyond reasonable doubt that: • the offender: • caused the victim’s death in company with two or more people; or • entered into an agreement, arrangement or understanding with two or more people to engage in the conduct that caused the victim’s death; and • the offender: • planned in advance to have and use an offensive weapon or firearm, and did use the offensive weapon or firearm to cause the victim’s death; or • planned in advance to engage in the conduct that caused the victim’s death and at the time of planning a reasonable person would have foreseen that the conduct would be likely to result in death; or • caused two or more serious injuries to the victim during a sustained or prolonged attack.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 9 – Statutory Schemes > 9.1 – Mandatory imprisonment schemes > 9.1.2 – Mandatory minimum sentences > 9.1.2.1 – Manslaughter offences – 10-year minimum non-parole period

refs.q: In addition, the minimum non-parole period for manslaughter by a single punch or strike does not apply to a person who intentionally directed, assisted or encouraged the offence, or who intentionally directed, assisted or encouraged another offence knowing it was probable the charged offence would occur.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 9 – Statutory Schemes > 9.1 – Mandatory imprisonment schemes > 9.1.2 – Mandatory minimum sentences > 9.1.2.1 – Manslaughter offences – 10-year minimum non-parole period

type: role, charges, plea, personal circumstances and sentence (including non-parole period) of each co-offender
title: Co-offenders and their sentences
statement: Parity requires any significant difference to be rationally explained, comparing all components.

refs.q: The concept is simply that when two or more co-offenders are sentenced, any significant difference in the sentences imposed upon them should be capable of a rational explanation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Comparison of the head sentence alone is not an adequate measure of parity. All components of the sentence (including any non-parole period) must be considered, and if totality requires different sentences between the co-offenders, then parity is not breached.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

field: offender.mental_health: condition, at offence / at sentence, expert reports, link to offending, self-induced intoxication; mental_illness_at_sentence (actual / apparent / none); intellectual_disability (with any DHS Secretary statement); DHS Secretary’s specification for a residential treatment order
type: structured with evidence references
title: Mental impairment and expert evidence
statement: Verdins, the Category 2 impaired-mental-functioning exceptions, mandatory minimum special reasons and mental health orders all require evidence of the condition at the relevant time and its effect. The mental health orders distinguish: a court assessment order needs only an apparent mental illness, a court secure treatment order an actual one at sentence; intellectual disability alone is not “mental illness” and an RTO or justice plan condition needs a DHS Secretary statement or specification.

refs.q: There needs to be cogent evidence, normally in the form of expert evidence, establishing on the balance of the probabilities that the Verdins principles are enlivened. The evidence must establish that the impairment existed at the time of offending, sentence, or both, as well as its nature, extent, and effect on the offender or its likely effect on them in the future. Expert evidence also needs to be assessed against what is known about the circumstances of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: this provision cannot apply if there is no extant mental illness at the time of sentence, only the possibility that one might be developed in prison;
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 9 – Statutory Schemes > 9.1 – Mandatory imprisonment schemes > 9.1.1 – Category 1 and 2 offences

refs.q: Orders under the Act can only be made if, among other requirements, the court is satisfied that the offender ‘appears to have a mental illness’ (in the case of a court assessment order) or in fact has a mental illness (in the case of a court secure treatment order).
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.1 – Mental illness

refs.q: In Victoria, ‘mental illness’ is a medical condition that is characterised by a significant disturbance of thought, mood, perception or memory. A person is not considered to have a mental illness only because they: • express, refuse, or fail to express a particular political opinion or belief; • express, refuse, or fail to express a particular religious opinion or belief; • express, refuse, or fail to express a particular philosophy; • express, refuse, or fail to express a particular sexual preference, gender identity or sexual orientation; • engage in, refuse, or fail to engage in a particular political activity; • engage in, refuse, or fail to engage in a particular religious activity; • engage in sexual promiscuity; • engage in immoral conduct; • engage in illegal conduct; • engage in antisocial behaviour; • are intellectually disabled; • use drugs or consume alcohol; • have a particular economic or social status or are a member of a particular cultural or racial group; • are or have previously been involved in family conflict; • have previously been treated for mental illness.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 15 – Court assessment and secure treatment orders > 15.1 – Mental illness

field: offender.addiction; offender.dependency_contributed; offender.intoxicated_by_liquor; offender.intoxicated_by_drug; intoxication_contributed; previous_aeo_for_offence
type: structured (each yes / no / unknown, with evidence)
title: Addiction and intoxication
statement: Addiction and intoxication bear on culpability, rehabilitation and the choice of sanction. A DATO needs a dependency on drugs or alcohol that contributed to the offence (balance of probabilities). An alcohol exclusion order is mandatory only where a conviction is recorded for a relevant offence, the offender was intoxicated by liquor (“intoxicated” refers to the consumption of liquor), the intoxication significantly contributed, and there has been no previous AEO for the offence.

refs.q: Lastly, an offender’s addiction may be relevant to the choice of sanction, either because it may qualify them for a sanction specifically tailored to their addiction or by emphasising the value of a general rehabilitative sanction.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.3 – Addictions

refs.q: Intoxication – whether through alcohol or narcotic consumption – will rarely mitigate offending, and may even be an aggravating factor. For intoxication to reduce moral culpability, the circumstances will have to be ‘quite exceptional’. The key question is the degree of foreknowledge. If the offender knew of the likely consequences of drug ingestion their culpability is increased, and intoxication may be an aggravating factor. Where a long history of alcohol consumption has not revealed the slightest indication that an offender poses a risk of violence, this may mean the circumstances are sufficiently exceptional to be mitigating.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.4 – Intoxication

refs.q: The Act provides that a court must make an AEO if: • it records a conviction against the offender for a relevant offence; and • it is satisfied on the balance of probabilities that: • at the time of the relevant offence the offender was intoxicated; and • the offender's intoxication significantly contributed to the commission of the relevant offence; and • the offender is not, or has not been, the subject of a previous AEO in relation to the current offence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 20 – Other ancillary orders > 20.1 – Alcohol related orders > 20.1.1 – Alcohol exclusion orders

refs.q: • the court is satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the offender is dependent on drugs or alcohol and that their dependency contributed to the commission of the offence
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 15A – Drug and Alcohol Treatment Orders > 15A.3 – Eligibility and limits

refs.q: Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) s 89DC (‘the Act’) defines ‘intoxicated’ as where ‘the person's speech, balance, coordination or behaviour is noticeably affected as a result of the consumption of liquor’.

type: structured with evidence references
title: Personal circumstances
statement: Childhood deprivation must be considered; employment history indicates rehabilitation prospects; ill health matters if it makes imprisonment more burdensome; third-party hardship needs exceptional circumstances (but see flag.third_party_hardship_exceptionality); Koori Court participation may mitigate. Whether to record a conviction requires the impact of a conviction on economic or social wellbeing or employment prospects; the need for a licence bears on the disqualification period.

refs.q: Bugmy has made clear that an offender’s circumstances and experiences of deprivation or violence during their childhood and formative years must be considered in sentencing – not just out of historical curiosity but because the effects of social disadvantage do not diminish with time.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

refs.q: The employment history of an offender is relevant during sentencing as it is an indication of their prospects for rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.2 – Employment

refs.q: The physical health or disability of the offender is relevant where: • imprisonment will be a greater burden because of their health; or • there is a serious risk of imprisonment having a grave effect on their health.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.1 – Physical health or disability

refs.q: Moreover, an Aboriginal offender’s participation in a Koori Court sentencing conversation may be mitigating because of various factors, including:
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.1 – Innate characteristics > 6.1.3 – Ethnicity, culture and race

refs.q: In deciding whether to record a conviction, a court must consider all the circumstances of the case including the nature of the offence, the character and history of the offender, and the impact of recording a conviction on their economic or social well-being, or employment prospects.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: A court must consider the disqualification period’s effect on rehabilitation and whether the period fixed would be counter-productive to its achievement.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.5 – Determining period of disqualification

type: structured with evidence references
title: Character, remorse and restitution
statement: Good character must be taken into account if established (subject to the child sexual offence exception); remorse must be proved by proper evidence; restitution is mitigating.

refs.q: If the evidence establishes that the offender is ‘otherwise of good character’ then, subject to a statutory exception, this must be taken into account in sentencing. However, the weight given to good character will vary according to the circumstances of the case and the offender, and in determining the weight to be given to previous good character there is no prohibition on a court considering the nature and circumstances of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.1 – Character > 6.3.1.1 – Good character

refs.q: An offender who wants to rely on remorse in mitigation must ‘satisfy the court there is genuine penitence and contrition and a desire to atone’. This must be established on proper evidence and a court should be cautious before accepting that an offender’s guilty plea indicates remorse warranting more than a utilitarian discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: but apart from that it is also a relevant factor at common law that allows for a sentence to be reduced or a shorter non-parole period to be fixed. But even full reparation does not entitle an offender to avoid all aspects of punishment.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.2 – Restitution

type: none | admissions | assistance given | undertaking to assist (nature, risk, evidence given)
title: Cooperation with authorities
statement: Assistance or an undertaking to assist affects the sentence, must be announced and recorded, and is an exception to the Category 2 and mandatory minimum regimes.

refs.q: Under the Victorian scheme, if a sentencing court imposes a less severe sentence than it otherwise would have because the offender has undertaken to assist law enforcement authorities, the court must both announce that it is doing this and have the details of the undertaking placed in the record. Failure to comply with these requirements does not automatically vitiate a sentencing exercise, but compliance with them remains important.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.3 – State v Commonwealth scheme > 7.3.3.1 – Identification of discount

field: dates: offence, interview, charge, plea, sentence; cause of delay; rehabilitation since
type: dates and evidence
title: Delay
statement: Delay may mitigate on either limb (unfairness, rehabilitation), each requiring some evidence; its cause matters.

refs.q: Significant delay between the time an offender is interviewed by police and the time charges are laid, as well as delay between the laying of charges and trial, can be a powerful mitigating factor. However, delay in itself creates no automatic right to a sentencing discount. The most that can be said is that where the prosecution unduly delays bringing the matter to court there is much more likely to be a discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay

refs.q: Where an offender relies on either limb of delay, they must provide some evidence to support the submission.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.1 – Evidence of delay

type: structured with evidence references
title: Conditions of custody; deportation risk; custody at sentence
statement: Protective custody and onerous conditions are relevant on evidence of actual effect; deportation is relevant only with evidence of its likelihood and impact; a court assessment order requires that the person is not in custody pending sentencing.

refs.q: In assessing the weight to be given to this factor, the court must assess the actual effect on the offender of their classification as a protection prisoner. The degree of restriction varies greatly from one case to the other.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.1 – Protection prisoners

refs.q: There must also be evidence of both the likely risk of deportation and the impact of that risk. Specifically, the evidence must be ‘sufficient to permit a sensible quantification of that risk to be undertaken’. A reduction will be permissible and appropriate where the prospect of deportation (and its impact) is certain. It may also be appropriate where deportation and its adverse impacts are probable.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

field: offences to be taken into account (s 100); uncharged conduct alleged
type: list
title: Offences taken into account and uncharged conduct
statement: Admitted pending offences may harden (not lengthen beyond the maximum) the sentence; uncharged conduct may not be punished as a separate or more serious offence.

refs.q: If offences are admitted and are to be considered, the court cannot impose more than the maximum penalty available for the offence(s) in respect of which sentence is formally being passed. Nor can it result in a lesser sentence. Instead it has the effect of hardening the sentence particularly if it is a serious offence. However, as general policy, this procedure should not be used for the disposal of serious offences.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.8 – Taking other offences into account

refs.q: Uncharged conduct or discreditable conduct may be treated as an aggravating feature of the offence, and as an indicator of increased moral culpability. But where the uncharged conduct constitutes an aggravated version of the offending or should have been alleged as a separate charge entirely, a court may not take it into account. Uncharged acts cannot be taken as aggravating factors where they warrant conviction for a more serious offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 5 – Circumstances and gravity of the offence > 5.2 – Statutory factors > 5.2.8 – Aggravating, mitigating, and other relevant circumstances > 5.2.8.5 – Uncharged conduct and surrounding facts

field: per charge: arising_from_driving (yes / no / unknown); under the influence of alcohol, or of alcohol and a drug; police pursuit; vehicle theft; RSA s 61(3) charge and any previous s 61(3) offence; licence status: Victorian licence or permit / interstate or overseas licence / none / unknown; current suspensions (including RSA Part 6B); licence history
type: structured
title: Driving-related facts (licence orders; driving-linked guidance)
statement: Serious motor vehicle offences require disqualification with a minimum period (cancellation for a Victorian licence or permit holder; the form follows the licence status); conviction for dangerous or negligent driving while pursued by police, and for vehicle theft, also requires disqualification; RSA s 61(3) requires cancellation and disqualification (4 or 2 years for a first offence, 8 or 4 for a subsequent one, depending on whether a conviction is recorded); other offences connected with driving allow discretionary disqualification. “Arising from driving” also decides whether the NCSI-by-driving guidance applies to a s 24 charge (s 24 is a generic offence).

refs.q: For dangerous driving causing death or serious injury, the minimum period of disqualification is 18 months. For a substance-influenced offence (other than aggravated carjacking), the minimum period of disqualification is 12 months. For any other serious motor vehicle offence, the minimum disqualification period is two years.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.1 – Mandatory disqualification

refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.2 – Discretionary licence disqualification

refs.q: Mandatory disqualification also follows if an offender has been convicted for: • dangerous or negligent driving while being pursued by police; or • stealing or attempting to steal a motor vehicle.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 16 – Licence disqualification > 16.1 – Mandatory disqualification

title: Financial circumstances, property and claims
statement: Means bear on a fine’s amount (after deciding to fine) and on compensation; the onus is on the offender to put material before the court about their financial circumstances. Confiscation and compensation orders interact with the sentence: each is made on application (personal injury compensation only on the injured person’s application); an offender relying on lawful acquisition must present credible material; the court may not take into account the automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property; personal injury compensation must be reduced by any VOCA Act award; own-motion property compensation is available only where the hearing commenced on or after 31 January 2013.

statement: Before making a detention order for a young offender charged with a Category A serious youth offence, or a Category B one with a prior Category A or B conviction, the court must be satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist. The Manual does not list the offences in each category (flag.serious_youth_offence_categories), so the user must supply them; unknown → caution.

refs.q: Before making a detention order for a young offender charged with a Category A Serious Youth Offence, or with a Category B Serious Youth Offence where they have also previously been convicted of a Category A or B Serious Youth Offence, a court must be satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist.

title: Sentencing after a retrial: the previous sentence
statement: When sentencing after a retrial the court must have regard to the sentence previously imposed; it is not bound by it, but cases where the second sentence may permissibly exceed the first will be rare (time may have changed the offender’s circumstances).

refs.q: When sentencing after a retrial, a court must have regard to the sentence previously imposed. It is not bound by it, but instances where the second sentence may permissibly exceed the first will be rare.
